<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhiqiu Xu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Amish Sethi
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mayur Naik
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Pennsylvania
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ser-Nam Lim
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Central Florida
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The success of powerful open source Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled the community to create a vast collection of post-trained models adapted to specific tasks and domains. However, navigating and understanding these models remains challenging due to inconsistent metadata and unstructured repositories. We introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Delta Activations</span>, a method to represent finetuned models as vector embeddings by measuring shifts in their internal activations relative to a base model. This representation allows for effective clustering by domain and task, revealing structure in the model landscape. Delta Activations also demonstrate desirable properties: it is robust across finetuning settings and exhibits an additive property when finetuning datasets are mixed. In addition, we show that Delta Activations can embed tasks via few-shot finetuning, and further explore its use for model selection and merging.
We hope Delta Activations can facilitate the practice of reusing publicly available models. Code is available at <a href="https://github.com/OscarXZQ/delta_activations" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/OscarXZQ/delta_activations</a>.</p>
  
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Equal contribution.</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Starting from powerful pretrained LLMs such as LLaMA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>, Gemma <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite>, Qwen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>, and DeepSeek <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, the community
has produced a vast and growing ecosystem of post-trained models—extensions that elicit diverse capabilities and knowledge from pretraining and are specialized for distinct tasks, domains, or human preferences.
This ecosystem spans models optimized through supervised finetuning (SFT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> on curated instruction datasets as well as those through preference alignment techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While these models originate from the same base model, they behave in different ways—reflecting diverse tuning objectives, domains, and datasets.
Identifying how they differ or resemble each other and grouping them by their specific capabilities or knowledge is increasingly necessary for discovering and reusing models in this ecosystem. Otherwise, these post-trained models would remain vastly underutilized, squandering the substantial energy invested in their training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2509.04442v1/embedding_space.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/147;" width="452" height="147"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Embedding Finetuned Models.<span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Can we project a pool of finetuned models into a vector space that captures similarities and differences in model behaviors and capabilities? Such a model embedding is useful for tasks that involve multiple models, like model selection and merging.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Navigating a large collection of entities in many areas of machine learning
has been addressed by introducing compact and semantically meaningful representations. Embeddings for <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">words</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">images</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, and <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">users</span> or <span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">items</span> in recommendation systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> provide a way to map these entities into continuous vector spaces that capture their underlying structure and relationships.
These representations reveal patterns and similarities that are often hidden in raw data which in turn enables a wide range of downstream applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In the landscape of post-trained LLMs, we lack a representation to efficiently discover, compare, and cluster <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">models</span> based on their finetuned behaviors and specializations. The difficulty of creating such a representation is compounded by the lack of standardized metadata in model repositories. Models are often ambiguously named, sparsely documented, and rarely linked to the datasets or objectives used during post-training—attributes that prior works rely upon for model characterization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce a model embedding method called <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Delta Activations</span> which provides a standalone representation derived solely from the model itself.
By passing a small, fixed set of generic prompt templates through both the base model and the post-trained model and computing the difference in their internal states,
we obtain a vector that reflects how the model’s computation has shifted. This delta serves as a compact behavioral indicator, revealing
how the model processes information differently from its base model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct experiments to demonstrate that Delta Activations form an effective embedding space that possesses desirable properties. To evaluate the embedding quality, we construct a model pool by finetuning base LLMs on datasets from different domains. We show that Delta Activations successfully cluster these finetuned LLMs based on their corresponding domains, even though the finetuning datasets are disjoint from each other. Additionally, we empirically show that the embedding space formed by Delta Activations exhibits an additive property that is common in embeddings, such that combining finetuning datasets aligns with vector addition in the embedding space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To validate the effectiveness of Delta Activations, we demonstrate its stability across different training settings and finetuning regimes, and apply Delta Activations to proof-of-concept model hubs to demonstrate its applications to model selection and model merging. Beyond this core method, our framework naturally generalizes to other choices of representation—what we refer to as <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Delta-X</span>—where the <math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> can be activations, logits, or meaning representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. In particular, when the underlying representation is model-agnostic, Delta-X enables embedding models finetuned from different base LLMs into a shared space. Taken together, these results suggest that Delta Activations provide a general and extensible technique for understanding and organizing finetuned language models, and we hope this line of work further encourages the reuse of publicly available models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Representing Models</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Problem setup</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{base}}</annotation></semantics></math> be a pretrained large language model and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}=\{f_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{K}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}=\{f_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{K}\}</annotation></semantics></math> be a set of finetuned models derived from <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{base}}</annotation></semantics></math> through post-training.
Our goal is to construct an embedding <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> for each model <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f\in\mathcal{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f\in\mathcal{F}</annotation></semantics></math> that reflects how the model specializes and behaves differently from <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{base}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Existing works and challenges</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several approaches have been proposed to represent LLMs: some rely on access to the original training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>, others apply dimensionality reduction over flattened weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite>, or construct embeddings from evaluation profiles <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>. However, each of these methods has limitations in real-world settings: Training-data-dependent representations require direct access to datasets, which are often proprietary or inaccessible.
In addition, such representations cannot differentiate models trained on the same data but with different training settings.
Dimensionality reduction on model weights assumes consistent adapter configurations across models, which is unrealistic constraint given the diversity of community-trained LLMs.
Finally, evaluation-based embeddings reflect only surface-level behavior, making them fragile to prompt variations and noisy in capturing true internal model shifts.
This motivates us to develop a technique that captures intrinsic model behavior independently.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>A simple experiment</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We finetune <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B</span> on 3 domains: <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Math</span>, <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Coding</span>, and <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Medical</span>. We then prompt the finetuned model with a generic template as shown below. Specifically, we use Alpaca <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite> instruction template, but without any real instruction or input.</p>
<blockquote id="S2.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">Below is an instruction that describes a task, paired with an input that provides further context. Write a response that appropriately completes the request.</span></p>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">### Instruction:</span><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">Please provide a response.</span><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">### Input:</span><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">Input.</span></p>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">### Response:</span></p>
</blockquote>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">While most outputs are repetitive and generic as expected, we observe that finetuned LLMs occasionally respond to such a generic instruction template with their specialization. We provide examples that show this behavior for each of these three models in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.3 A simple experiment ‣ 2 Representing Models ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span><span id="S2.T1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompting finetuned LLMs with generic inputs.</span> Sometimes finetuned LLMs produce outputs that reveal their specialization in spite of the prompt being completely generic.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">From this observation, we conjecture that:</p>
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.SS3.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A generic instruction template may elicit certain specialization behavior in a finetuned LLM</span>.</p>
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">This phenomenon may be explainable by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren &amp; Sutherland [53]</a></cite>, which studies how finetuning on one data point may steer LLM’s response on other data points. Although directly representing models with these outputs does not work well, as our experiments in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> and Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> show, this observation naturally leads to our method Delta Activations where we instead use <span id="S2.SS3.p2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">activations</span> from the generic instruction template to represent finetuned LLMs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Delta Activations</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S2.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Delta Activations</span>, a method to represent finetuned language models as vector embeddings by measuring the difference in their hidden states compared to a fixed base model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2509.04442v1/methodology.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/140;" width="476" height="140"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Illustration of computing Delta Activations.<span id="S2.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The difference between a finetuned model’s hidden state and the base model’s hidden state on a shared input quantifies the effect of finetuning.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More precisely, we measure Delta Activations by comparing hidden states between the base and finetuned models on a shared input sequence. Let <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{f}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{f}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the last token’s activation from the final layer of model <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> for an input <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. We define the Delta Activations as:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{f}(x)=h^{f}(x)-h^{\text{base}}(x)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{f}(x)=h^{f}(x)-h^{\text{base}}(x)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{f}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{f}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> quantifies how the model’s internal representation of the input <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> diverges from the base model as a result of finetuning. To construct the model’s embedding, we aggregate the Delta Activations over a fixed probe dataset <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{probe}}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{N}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>probe</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{probe}}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{N}\}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{f}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{f}(x_{i})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{f}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{f}(x_{i})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Probe dataset.</span> Motivated by the above experiment and the need for a universally applicable embedding method, the probe dataset <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{probe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>probe</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{probe}}</annotation></semantics></math> is explicitly designed to be <span id="S2.SS4.p2.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">completely generic</span>, aiming to activate core computational pathways in the model without bias toward specific tasks or domains. Therefore, we start with the Alpaca template populated with dummy instruction and inputs (as shown in Section <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 A simple experiment ‣ 2 Representing Models ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>) as the first data point in the probe dataset. The rest of the probe dataset is generated through paraphrasing by GPT-4o, maintaining the simplicity and generic nature of the template while introducing linguistic diversity. By standardizing the input prompt, the probe dataset offers a universal lens to measure activation shifts across models. We use <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{probe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>probe</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{probe}}</annotation></semantics></math> in our main setting,
and further study the effects of the size, length, and content of the input prompts in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Notable benefits.</span> Delta Activations naturally comes with many advantages. Firstly, for new incoming models, it only takes one forward pass to compute the embedding for a model, taking much less computation than evaluation-based method. In addition, Delta Activations does not change embeddings of existing models like previous methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>, which represent models jointly by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or matrix factorization. Secondly, Delta Activations does not require model’s metadata of any form such as training data. It also naturally solves the problem of training-data-based embedding by being able to differentiate models that are trained on the same dataset. Finally, Delta Activations can also be used to represent tasks, as we describe next.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Few-shot task embedding.</span> Delta Activations can be seamlessly extended to represent a given task. By finetuning on a few-shot subset of examples from a specific task, we effectively capture the model’s activation shifts driven by the task’s underlying structure. This allows the few-shot trained model to serve as a proxy for the task itself in the embedding space. Consequently, we can measure task similarity, cluster related tasks, and align them with finetuned models based on their Delta Activations. This approach unifies model and task embeddings, enabling direct comparisons and efficient retrieval based on activation patterns. We evaluate the task embedding in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Extensions ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Beyond Activations: the Delta-X family.</span> While Delta Activations serve as our primary method, the framework naturally extends to a family of delta-based representations. Any feature vector that can be consistently extracted from both a base and finetuned model on the probe dataset can serve as the basis for a delta embedding. This flexibility gives rise to variants such as <em id="S2.SS4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Delta Logits</em>, <em id="S2.SS4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Delta Weighted Activations</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, and <em id="S2.SS4.p5.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Delta Meaning</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. Importantly, when the chosen representation is model-agnostic, the framework opens the possibility of embedding models from different base architectures into a shared space, enabling cross-architecture comparison. We evaluate these variants in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> and explore embedding difference base LLMs in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Extensions ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Delta Activations as a model embedding by evaluating clustering quality across multiple model pools, analyzing its properties, and exploring its potential for broader applications.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Delta Activations as a Model Embedding</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model pool construction.</span> We build three model pools, each originating from a different pretrained base model: <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Gemma-2-9B</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite>, and <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Qwen-2.5-7B</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>. Each pool contains 15 finetuned models—three per domain across five domains: <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Legal</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Math</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Medical</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Commonsense</span>, and <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Coding</span>. We assign one dataset per domain and create three disjoint splits with 3000 examples each for supervised finetuning. We use LegalBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> for <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Legal</span>, GSM-8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> for <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Math</span>, PubMedQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> for <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Medical</span>, HellaSwag <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>]</cite> for <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Commonsense</span>, and OPC-SFT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> for <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Coding</span>. We finetune all models for three epochs using LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> with learning rate set to <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1e^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1e^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> and batch size 4 by default. See Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Training settings ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> for all finetuning settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metric.</span> We evaluate clustering quality using the silhouette score <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>, defined for each model <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max(a(i),b(i))}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max(a(i),b(i))}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a(i)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(i)</annotation></semantics></math> is the average distance to models in the same cluster, and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(i)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(i)</annotation></semantics></math> is the average distance to the nearest other cluster. Scores range from <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> (misclustered) to <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+1</annotation></semantics></math> (well-clustered); we report the average over all models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span> We compare Delta Activations against the following three alternative methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flattened weights:</span> As a basic parameter-space baseline, we flatten the weights of the finetuned LoRA adapters directly into a high-dimensional vector representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Salient mask:</span> Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al. [17]</a></cite>, we adopt the binary mask variant of Localize-and-Stitch, where each model is represented by a <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0/1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0/1</annotation></semantics></math> vector marking the top <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\%</annotation></semantics></math> most salient parameters with the largest finetuning updates. This representation captures <em id="S3.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where</em> adaptation occurs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Output sentence embeddings:</span> Motivated by Section <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 A simple experiment ‣ 2 Representing Models ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>, we use a standard sentence embedding model, <span id="S3.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">All-MiniLM-L6-v2</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>, to encode the finetuned models’ generated outputs on the same generic probe dataset used by Delta Activations. Recent works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite> also show that outputs from different LLMs are highly distinguishable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span> As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, Delta Activations achieves strongest clustering performance across all backbones. Flattened weights fail to form effective clusters as shown by its negative silhouette score.
Output sentence embeddings succeed in forming clusters for LLaMA but not for Gemma or Qwen, showing that the generic probe dataset does not always elicit model specializations in the word space, in contrast to the consistent results of Delta Activations. The t-SNE visualization for Gemma, presented in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, further illustrates these findings, showing that weight-based methods fail to form any cluster whereas output sentence embeddings occasionally form wrong clusters. Delta Activations form correct clusters across all domains.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.T2.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S3.T2.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T2.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Embedding Space</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T2.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Dimension</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T2.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">LLaMA</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T2.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Gemma</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T2.3.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Qwen</span></td>

<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Understanding Delta Activations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we investigate properties of Delta Activations, analyze probe datasets and activation selection, and validate its stability over different training settings and finetuning regimes. Unless otherwise noted, we report average silhouette score across three backbone model pools: <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B</span>, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Gemma-2-9B</span>, and <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Qwen-2.5-7B</span>. For all tables, the main setting is marked in <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">gray</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Delta-X variants.</span> Our framework is not limited to activations, but can generalize to other model features extracted from the probe dataset. We create and evaluate two variants of Delta Activations: <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Delta Logits</em>, and <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Delta Meaning</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> (differences in inverse perplexity scores over sampled continuations, implementation details in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS5" title="A.5 Delta Meaning implementation ‣ Appendix A Training settings ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a>). Results are shown in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Both these variants achieve reasonable clustering quality on our main experiment setting.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.T3.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">

<th id="S3.T3.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T3.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Dimensionality</span></th>
<th id="S3.T3.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T3.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">silh. score</span></th></tr>

<td id="S3.T3.3.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T3.3.4.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">.61</span></td></tr>

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span><span id="S3.T3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Delta-X.</span> Both variants achieve positive silhouette score in our main experiment setting, showing that our framework can be generalized to other representation extraction methods.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Additive property.</span> A function <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is additive if <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)</annotation></semantics></math> for any inputs <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>. We explore whether Delta Activations exhibits this property by examining whether the following holds.</p>
<table id="S3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\big(\text{model finetuned on }D_{1}\cup D_{2}\big)\approx v\big(\text{model finetuned on }D_{1}\big)+v\big(\text{model finetuned on }D_{2}\big)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>model finetuned on </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mtext>model finetuned on </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mtext>model finetuned on </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\big(\text{model finetuned on }D_{1}\cup D_{2}\big)\approx v\big(\text{model finetuned on }D_{1}\big)+v\big(\text{model finetuned on }D_{2}\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the operation to take Delta Activations. We finetune models on pairs of domains and comparing their Delta Activations to those from individually trained models. Results are presented in Table <a href="#S3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, which shows that the similarity between the mixed model and the sum of Delta Activations from the two individual models is consistently higher than the similarity with either individual model. This suggests that Delta Activations exhibit the additive property–combining shifts from separately finetuned models approximates the shift seen when trained on combined data. The additive structure in the embedding space is especially important since models are often trained on mixed datasets, ensuring that the embedding space preserves the influence of each component. We report results across all ten domain pairs in Appendix <a href="#A2.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ B.2 Full Results for Additive Properties experiment ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, where the additive effect consistently holds.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T4" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.T4.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S3.T4.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T4.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T4.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Math</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T4.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Commonsense</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T4.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Code</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T4.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Mixed vs. D1</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T4.3.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Mixed vs. D2</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.1.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T4.3.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Mixed vs. Sum(D1, D2)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T4.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T4.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T4.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T4.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_border_t"></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T4.3.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.58</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T4.3.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.48</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T4.3.2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">.65</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T4.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T4.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.3.2" class="ltx_td"></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.70</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.3.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.27</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.3.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">.73</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T4.3.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T4.3.4.1" class="ltx_td"></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.4.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>

<td id="S3.T4.3.4.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.4.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.28</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.3.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T4.3.4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">.65</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span><span id="S3.T4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Additive property.</span> The sum of Delta Activations on models finetuned separately on two datasets aligns well with Delta Activations on the model finetuned on two datasets mixed together.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Probe dataset.</span> We study the effects of number, length, and content of prompts in Table <a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
In (a), we see that using multiple prompts instead of one helps stabilize the embedding, while increasing the number from 5 to 20 offers no additional benefits. In (b), we see that using GPT-4o to generate shorter versions of the Alpaca template, namely one-word and one-sentence versions, performs worse than a reasonably long instruction template. All prompts used in this part are included in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Prompt Templates ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.
Finally, (c) shows the importance of a generic instruction template by comparing the instruction template with domain-specific prompts or Wikitext. Domain-specific prompts perform worst since they suppress the model’s specialization and thereby cause model embeddings to become less distinguishable. A random generic text sampled from Wikitext performs slightly better while the instruction template achieves the best separation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">These findings across prompt number, length, and content bolster our design choices for the probe dataset. In addition, even with variations in these prompt settings, the effectiveness of Delta Activations is preserved, as evident from the fact that the silhouette scores stay well above zero.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span><span id="S3.T5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effects of number, length, and content of probe prompts.</span> Using multiple reasonably-long generic instruction templates makes the best probe dataset.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Where to extract activations.</span> The embedding of the last token at the last layer is generally understood to encode the entire context. Decoder-only LLMs project this embedding to the logit space for next-token prediction. Consequently, Delta Activations are also derived using this embedding.
Here we study whether Delta Activations could instead be sourced from other tokens or different layers.
In Table <a href="#S3.T6.st1" title="In Table 6 ‣ 3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a>, we examine the effectiveness of calculating Delta Activations using the first, middle, and last tokens, as well as from the weighted average of all token embeddings following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Muennighoff [45]</a></cite>. Overall, the results show that final tokens are effective targets for calculating Delta Activations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We also investigate whether the final layer is the best position from which to extract activations. As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T6.st2" title="In Table 6 ‣ 3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(b)</span></a>, shallower layers perform worse than deeper ones; interestingly, the final layer is not optimal, as a layer at <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/3</annotation></semantics></math> of the total depth performs best. This phenomenon, where intermediate representation are found to be more effective for downstream tasks, is also observed in vision encoders <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. Although a layer at <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/3</annotation></semantics></math> depth and weighted tokens exhibit slightly superior results, the final token at the last layer performs similarly. For simplicity, we use the last-layer final token embedding as the default setting for Delta Activations.</p>
</div>

<td id="S3.T6.st2.3.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T6.st2.3.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">deep (2/3 depth)</span></td>
<td id="S3.T6.st2.3.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T6.st2.3.4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">.64</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T6.st2.3.5" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">
<td id="S3.T6.st2.3.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T6.st2.3.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">last</span></td>
<td id="S3.T6.st2.3.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T6.st2.3.5.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">.61</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">(b) </span>layer position</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span><span id="S3.T6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effects of token and layer position to extract activations.</span> Later tokens and deeper layeres produce better Delta Activations, with the <math id="S3.T6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/3</annotation></semantics></math> depth layer slightly surpassing the last layer.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Robustness to training settings.</span> Do differences in training settings have a greater impact on Delta Activations than the choice of finetuned domains? To evaluate this, we systematically perturbed the training process for models within our domain clusters. In our main setting, the model pool is organized into 5 distinct domain clusters, with 3 models in each cluster trained using identical settings. To test the impact of a specific training configuration—for instance, learning rate—the three models within each of the 5 domain clusters were trained using three different learning rates respectively (e.g., model 1 with <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1e^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1e^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, model 2 with <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4e^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4e^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, model 3 with <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1e^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1e^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> within a single domain cluster). This process was independently repeated for variations in the number of training examples and the number of training epochs, where we vary number of training examples by 100, 1000, and 10000 and number of epochs by 1, 2, and 3.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> presents results which measure the clustering quality on domains when subjected to such training variations. indicates that varied training settings generally did not break domain-specific clustering. Changes to the amount of training data or the number of epochs had minimal effect on the quality of these clusters, which remained comparable to those formed under identical training settings.
The different-learning-rate setting yields a lower silhouette score, as expected, since learning rate significantly impacts training dynamics and tends to increase within-cluster variation. These observations confirm that Delta Activations effectively identify finetuning domains despite common variations in training procedures. On the other hand, these results also show the strength of Delta Activations in identifying the nuanced differences within each cluster.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T7" class="ltx_table">

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span><span id="S3.T7.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Delta Activations’ embeddings are robust to training hyperparameters.</span> Models trained in varying settings still form tight domain-specific clusters, comparable to those trained identically.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Beyond domains: clustering by dataset properties.</span> In our setting in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, each domain corresponds to a well-defined task with relatively uniform answer structure (e.g., multiple-choice). Here, we ablate that structure. We construct a new model pool by finetuning 3 models on each of five distinct subsets of <span id="S3.SS2.p10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Tulu v2</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>: <span id="S3.SS2.p10.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CoT</span>, <span id="S3.SS2.p10.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">GPT4-Alpaca</span>, <span id="S3.SS2.p10.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ShareGPT</span>, <span id="S3.SS2.p10.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CodeAlpaca</span>, and <span id="S3.SS2.p10.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Science</span>. Unlike domain datasets, these are less semantically disjoint. Instead, they differ in instruction format, conversational structure, and expected output style—ranging from open-ended dialogue to multi-step chain-of-thought reasoning, code snippets, and longform factual answers. Crucially, this makes the output distribution far more diverse and less predictable. Results are presented in Table <a href="#S3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. With no consistent answer template, output sentence embeddings fail to reflect model specialization for LLaMA and Qwen, whereas Delta Activations continue to achieve decent clustering quality.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T8" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.T8.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span><span id="S3.T8.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Clustering quality (silhouette score) across Tulu v2 instruction splits.</span> Delta Activations remain effective despite diverse output structures and blurred instruction boundaries.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Beyond SFT: clustering by preference optimization.</span> Our experiments thus far focused on the setting of Supervised Finetuning which use the token-level cross entropy loss. Preference optimization techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> maximize the likelihood that preferred responses are ranked higher. The different supervision signal of preference optimization affects the activation differently. We explore whether Delta Activations still yield reliable clustering for models in this case. To construct the model pool, we perform preference optimization on <span id="S3.SS2.p11.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct</span> using three disjoint 3000-example splits for each of three preference optimization datasets, namely UltraFeedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, HumanLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and MetaMath-DPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>. This experiment yields a silhouette score of <span id="S3.SS2.p11.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.93</span>, which shows that Delta Activations can effectively capture similarity for preference optimization.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F5.fig1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Preference optimization.<span id="S3.F5.fig1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Delta Activations can cluster models trained with DPO.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
