<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S3.F5.fig2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Task embedding.<span id="S3.F5.fig2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Few-shot task embedding is able to locate model clusters.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Extensions</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we explore how Delta Activations as a model embedding can be extended to embedding a task, representing LLMs finetuned from different base LLMs, and guiding model merging.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task embedding.</span> We explore whether Delta Activations can embed tasks using only a few examples—a setting analogous to few-shot generalization. For each of the five domains in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we finetune the base LLM on 20 held-out examples that were not part of any previous training split. The detailed few-shot finetuning setting is in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Few-shot Task Embedding Configuration ‣ Appendix A Training settings ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a>. We then embed the few-shot finetuned models using Delta Activations, and use this embedding as a representation of the task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We examine whether the task embedding can successfully locate the corresponding clusters on the three model pools constructed in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>. We define the <em id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">retrieval rate</em> metric as the fraction of few-shot task embeddings that correctly retrieve their corresponding full-model cluster via nearest-neighbour search using cosine similarity. Gemma achieves 100% retrieval rate while there is one failure case for each of LLaMA and Qwen. We present visualization of Gemma in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.2 Understanding Delta Activations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, which shows that few-shot queries reliably align with their corresponding full model clusters (circles). Despite being trained on only 20 examples, the resulting Delta Activations recover the domain cluster. This suggests that Delta Activations on few-shot trained model can be an effective task embedding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-base-model clustering.</span>
Delta Activations represent a finetuned model as the difference between its hidden states and those of its base model on the same inputs; therefore, they can only be directly applied to models derived from the <em id="S3.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">same</em> base. Interestingly, we find that this delta signal can transfer across bases. To test this, we evaluate two settings: cross-checkpoint and cross-architecture. In a cross-checkpoint setting (<span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3-8B</span> vs. <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B</span>; 10 models over 5 domains), Delta Activations achieved a silhouette score of <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.39</span>, cleanly recovering the five domain-specialization clusters (Figure <a href="#S3.F6.sf1" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 3.3 Extensions ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a>). In a cross-architecture setting (<span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B</span> vs. <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.2-1B</span>; 10 models), Delta Activations are no longer feasible because the embedding dimension differs across architectures, projecting models into vectors of incompatible sizes. Instead, we adopt <em id="S3.SS3.p4.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Delta Meaning</em> (full implementation details in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS5" title="A.5 Delta Meaning implementation ‣ Appendix A Training settings ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a>), which is architecture-agnostic, and it successfully forms four out of five domain clusters with a silhouette score of <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.32</span> (Figure <a href="#S3.F6.sf2" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 3.3 Extensions ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(b)</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F6.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2509.04442v1/cross_arch_3130.svg" id="S3.F6.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/281;" width="476" height="281"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F6.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S3.F6.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">cross-checkpoint</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F6.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2509.04442v1/cross_arch_8b1b.svg" id="S3.F6.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/281;" width="476" height="281"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F6.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S3.F6.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">cross-architecture</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F6.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S3.F6.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Cross-base-model clustering.<span id="S3.F6.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
(a) Delta Activations form domain clusters across models finetuned from <span id="S3.F6.9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B</span> and <span id="S3.F6.9.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3-8B</span>.
(b) Delta Meaning form domain clusters across finetuned models of different sizes, <span id="S3.F6.9.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B</span> and <span id="S3.F6.9.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.2-1B</span>.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model selection.</span> LoraHub <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> hosts <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 200</annotation></semantics></math> finetuned models based on <span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FLAN-T5</span>. The method is evaluated on the Big-Bench Hard (BBH) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>. For each task in BBH, LoraHub randomly select 20 LoRAs and optimizes their merging coefficients over few-shot examples from the target task. Our approach can be easily applied to this scenario by embedding the corresponding task using the provided few-shot examples and leverage Delta Activations similarity to replace the random model selection. Specifically, we identify the single most-related LoRA model as an anchor and samples the remaining 19 models randomly. This simple selection strategy enabled by Delta Activations yields an average performance improvement of 2.0% by boosting the average accuracy from 34.3% to 36.3% on the 26 tasks of the BBH benchmark. Interestingly, selecting 20 most similar models using Delta Activations yield an average performance of 30.3%, which is far lower than random selection. We conjecture that this is due to model interference identified by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ortiz-Jimenez et al. [47]</a></cite>, where similar models are entangled with each other, resulting in bad merging performance. However, this in turn shows that Delta Activations are informative about the relationships between models. While model merging is beyond the scope of our work, Delta Activations enable model merging strategies beyond nearest-neighbour selection. Our proof-of-concept experiment focused on simple selection strategies, but Delta Activations could be leveraged for more sophisticated approaches. For instance, one could use Delta Activations to identify a maximally dispersed subset of models to mitigate interference or train a neural network on top of Delta Activations embeddings to optimize merging decisions.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Embedding Models and Tasks.</span>
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al. [23]</a></cite> discovers that task vectors from finetuning can be merged to achieve multi-task learning.
There are several attempts to represent LLMs using adapter weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>, evaluation profiles <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>, or training-data-dependent characteristics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite>, but these methods rely on potentially inaccessible data or fail to reflect internal behavior. Our work differs by requiring no external supervision or evaluation, instead deriving embeddings from internal behaviors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Activations.</span>
Recent work uncovers structure in hidden activations of LLMs, understanding how massive activation act as biases to steer LLM output <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
Activations are also central to post-training compression: they are used to compute weight saliency for pruning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite> and to reduce quantization error using calibration sets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>]</cite>, which inspire the use of the probe dataset of Delta Activations. Additionally, learned activation shifts have been used to edit or transfer behavior across models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Utilizing trained models.</span>
The landscape evolves from reusing a single model to multiple trained models. Finetuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>]</cite> is a common framework to build on top of a single pretrained model, which becomes the common practice for LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>. Other works use outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> or weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> of a pretrained model for the creation or initialization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>, <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite> of more efficient models.
Efforts are made to effectively leverage multiple trained models through retrieval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, composition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, or routing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Buiding model hubs.</span> Recent works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite> study the public model pool and can systematically uncover finetuning relationship among trained models. Lorahub <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, LoraRetriever <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite>, and Learnware <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite> create model hubs involving from <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 40</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 200</annotation></semantics></math> models. It is also possible to create larger model hubs via neural network parameter diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, though achieving true diversity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite> may require further development.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Delta Activations provide a simple yet powerful way to represent finetuned LLMs by measuring shifts in their internal activations relative to a base LLM. Our experiments show that this representation consistently forms distinct clusters that reflect finetuning domains and offer the advantage of an additive property that mirrors multi-domain behavior. The stability of Delta Activations across varying finetuning settings shows its reliability for use-cases of model selection and merging in model hubs. We believe that Delta Activations can serve as a cornerstone for navigating the expanding landscape of finetuned models by enabling more efficient model discovery and reuse.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations and future work.</span> Delta Activations introduces a novel way to represent finetuned models but also poses practical considerations. Our experiments focused on three prominent open-source backbones but further evaluation on other architectures would be valuable to understand its broader applicability. In addition, Delta Activations require access to internal hidden states, which is not feasible to be evaluated on proprietary models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">It is natural to ask how our method might perform on model pools substantially larger than those considered in our evaluation. Such a practical exercise would be most meaningful if the pool consists of models with diverse and uniquely valuable capabilities. While this is an interesting direction we intend to explore, we conjecture that today such pools exist primarily in proprietary settings (e.g. finetuned GPT models), and we hope our approach could facilitate sharing such models in future.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Training settings</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For LoRA, we set rank <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=8</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=16</annotation></semantics></math>, targeting query, key, value, and MLP projections (<span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">q_proj</span>, <span id="A1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">k_proj</span>, <span id="A1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">v_proj</span>, <span id="A1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">up_proj</span>, <span id="A1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">down_proj</span>, <span id="A1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gate_proj</span>), with no dropout and no bias parameters.</p>
</div>

<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Few-shot Task Embedding Configuration</h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the few-shot task embedding experiments described in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Extensions ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, we used a configuration tailored for limited data scenarios. We randomly sampled 20 examples from each domain’s held-out data that was not used in any of our main experiment splits.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T12" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A1.T12.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A1.T12.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T12.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="A1.T12.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Parameter</span></th>
<td id="A1.T12.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t"><span id="A1.T12.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Value</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T12.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T12.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="A1.T12.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Examples per domain</span></th>
<td id="A1.T12.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t"><span id="A1.T12.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">20 (randomly sampled)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T12.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T12.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row"><span id="A1.T12.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Learning rate</span></th>
<td id="A1.T12.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="A1.T12.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">3.3e-3</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T12.3.4" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T12.3.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row"><span id="A1.T12.3.4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Batch size</span></th>
<td id="A1.T12.3.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="A1.T12.3.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T12.3.5" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T12.3.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_b"><span id="A1.T12.3.5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Epochs</span></th>
<td id="A1.T12.3.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b"><span id="A1.T12.3.5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">5</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 12: </span>Hyperparameters for few-shot task embedding experiments.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We maintained the same LoRA configuration as in our main experiments. The higher learning rate and increased number of epochs compensate for the limited training data while the smaller batch size allows for more frequent parameter updates. After fine-tuning, we computed Delta Activations using identical probe datasets as in our main experiments to ensure direct comparability between few-shot task embeddings and full model embeddings in the embedding space.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.5 </span>Delta Meaning implementation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here we provide implementation details for <span id="A1.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Delta Meaning</span>, our adaptation of Meaning Representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> to the Delta framework. This extension enables model embeddings across heterogeneous backbones, where direct activation comparisons are infeasible.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Meaning representations.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a probe prompt <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, we first sample <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> continuations <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{s_{1},\dots,s_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{s_{1},\dots,s_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math> from the base model (temperature = 1.0). For any finetuned model <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, we then score each continuation <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> by computing its inverse perplexity under <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="m_{f}(x)_{i}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{|s_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|s_{i}|}\log p_{f}(s_{i,t}\mid s_{i,&lt;t},x)\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></munderover><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{f}(x)_{i}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{|s_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|s_{i}|}\log p_{f}(s_{i,t}\mid s_{i,&lt;t},x)\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This produces an <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional “meaning vector” <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{f}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{f}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> for each prompt <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Delta aggregation.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a finetuned model <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> and its base <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{base}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define the <span id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Delta Meaning</span> on prompt <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> as the difference between their meaning vectors:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{f}(x)=m_{f}(x)-m_{f_{\text{base}}}(x)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{f}(x)=m_{f}(x)-m_{f_{\text{base}}}(x).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Aggregating across all prompts <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in D_{\text{probe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>probe</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in D_{\text{probe}}</annotation></semantics></math> yields the final model embedding:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{f}=\frac{1}{|D_{\text{probe}}|}\sum_{x\in D_{\text{probe}}}\Delta_{f}(x)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>probe</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>probe</mtext></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{f}=\frac{1}{|D_{\text{probe}}|}\sum_{x\in D_{\text{probe}}}\Delta_{f}(x).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hyperparameters.</span>
In our experiments, we set <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> to be 20. Larger <math id="A1.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> provides more informative embeddings but requires proportionally more forward passes, as each continuation must be scored by both the base and finetuned models. Despite this, the dimensionality of Delta Meaning remains extremely compact compared to weight- or logit-based alternatives. Importantly, because any model can evaluate the probability of a given text sequence, Delta Meaning embeddings are naturally architecture-agnostic, allowing us to cluster finetuned models drawn from multiple backbones.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
</section>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show visualization of the experiments conducted in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> on LLaMA and Qwen in Figure <a href="#A2.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ B.1 t-SNE Visualization on more backbones ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and Figure <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ B.1 t-SNE Visualization on more backbones ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> respectively. Over different backbones, the visualization consistently shows the superiority of Delta Activations in forming cleanly-separated clusters.</p>

<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Full Results for Additive Properties experiment</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand the additive nature of Delta Activations, we extend the experiment from Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> to cover all ten domain pairs. In each case, we compare the Delta Activation vector from a model trained on the mixed dataset against those from models trained individually on each domain, as well as their vector sum. This comprehensive table demonstrates that the summed Delta Activations consistently better approximate the mixed-model embedding, reinforcing the additive property of Delta Activations.</p>
</div>

<td id="A2.T13.3.11.4" class="ltx_td"></td>
<td id="A2.T13.3.11.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r"><span id="A2.T13.3.11.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>
<td id="A2.T13.3.11.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="A2.T13.3.11.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.445</span></td>
<td id="A2.T13.3.11.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="A2.T13.3.11.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.507</span></td>
<td id="A2.T13.3.11.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="A2.T13.3.11.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">.587</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 13: </span><span id="A2.T13.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Additive property (full).</span> The sum of Delta Activations on models finetuned separately on two datasets aligns well with Delta Activations on the model finetuned on two datasets mixed together.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Full finetuning</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct experiments in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Delta Activations as a Model Embedding ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> on <span id="A2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLaMA-3.1-8B</span> with the model pool trained using full finetuning instead of LoRA. This experiment yields a silhouette score of <span id="A2.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.63</span>, which confirms that Delta Activations provide clear clustering regardless of finetuning methods. Visualization is shown in Figure <a href="#A2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ B.3 Full finetuning ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2509.04442v1/fft.svg" id="A2.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/166;" width="333" height="166"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A2.F9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">t-SNE visualization of full finetuning.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Intra-domain clustering.</span> We conduct experiments to test whether Delta Activations provide sufficient signal to differentiate models trained on different sub-expertises within medical and coding domains.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We partition each domain into multiple sub-expertise splits. For medical, we create finetuned 8 models: disease databases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> (2 splits), disease-symptoms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> (2 splits), MedQA-USMLE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> (2 splits), and MedMCQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> (2 splits). For coding, we create 6 models covering C++ (2 splits), Python (2 splits), and Java (2 splits) from CodeChef <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, Codeforces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, and Evol-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> datasets. We compute Delta Activations using both generic instruction prompts and domain-specialized prompts.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ B.3 Full finetuning ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis ‣ Delta Activations: A Representation for Finetuned Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> shows that generic prompts achieve a silhouette score of 0.657 for medical sub-expertise, outperforming specialized medical prompts (0.533). For coding, both prompts perform comparably (0.668 vs 0.674). The generic probe maintains sufficient resolution to form correct clusters of sub-expertises within domains.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T14" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A2.T14.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">

</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Broader Impact</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The proposed Delta Activations method facilitate efficient reuse of fine-tuned models by providing an embedding to encode the finetuned model’s behaviors and capability. This reduces redundant training, cutting energy costs and promoting sustainable AI practices. Furthermore, it encourages broader public sharing of fine-tuned models by offering clear documentation of their capabilities, accelerating research and collaboration.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, expanding public model hubs also introduces risks, as low-quality or adversarial models could contaminate the pool. This highlights the need for careful curation to maintain reliability and safety in open model ecosystems.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
